title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 211
paragraphs: When the Medes were being roughly handled, they withdrew from the battle, and the Persians — those whom the king called the “Immortals,” commanded by Hydarnes — took their place and came up to attack, supposing that at least they would easily overcome the enemy. But when they too engaged the Greeks, they had no more success than the Medes — exactly the same — since they were fighting in a cramped pass, using shorter spears than the Greeks and unable to take advantage of their greater numbers. The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, fought memorably. Among other feats, being perfectly skilled warriors facing unskilled foes, they would turn their backs to the enemy and feign flight; and the barbarians, seeing them apparently fleeing, would chase after them with shouts and clashing of arms. Then, just as the Lacedaemonians were about to be caught, they would wheel and face the barbarians — and in this turn they would cut down countless multitudes of Persians. A few of the Spartans themselves also fell on these occasions. Since the Persians were unable to achieve any success, whether by attacking the entrance in divisions or by any other means, they pulled back.
